question: A company has a policy where engineers must only provision approved AWS resources using AWS CloudFormation. The solutions architect needs to enforce this restriction on the IAM role that the engineers use to provision resources. How can the solutions architect implement this policy?

options.text: Upload CloudFormation templates containing approved resources to an S3 bucket, and update the engineers' IAM policy to allow access to only CloudFormation and the S3 bucket.
Update the engineers' IAM policy to restrict access to only approved resources and AWS CloudFormation, and use CloudFormation templates to provision the resources.
Update the engineers' IAM policy to only allow AWS CloudFormation actions, create a service role to provision approved resources, and assign it to AWS CloudFormation during stack creation.
Create CloudFormation stacks with only approved resources and restrict engineers to provision only their stacks.

explanation: The book's answer key selects B, restricting the engineers' IAM policy to CloudFormation plus the approved resource set so that both the provisioning channel and the resource types are constrained. Note that option C describes the stronger and more commonly recommended pattern: engineers hold only CloudFormation permissions, and a CloudFormation service role carries the resource-creation permissions, which prevents provisioning outside of CloudFormation entirely. Option A controls template storage but not what engineers can create. Option D removes the engineers' ability to provision at all rather than constraining it, so this item is worth reviewing critically.

question: A company is building an application that will receive millions of small records (less than 4 KB each) from devices globally. The records need to be stored durably and accessed with low latency. The storage requirements will be 10-15 TB per year, and the data needs to be retained for 120 days prior to being deleted. What is the most cost-effective storage strategy to meet these requirements?

options.text: Store each incoming record as a single .csv file in Amazon S3, allow for indexed retrieval, and configure a lifecycle policy to delete data older than 120 days.
Store each incoming record in an Amazon DynamoDB table, and use the Time to Live (TTL) feature to delete records succeeding 120 days.
Store each record in an Amazon RDS MySQL database, and run a nightly cron job to delete records older than 120 days.
Batch incoming records prior to storing them in Amazon S3, use S3 metadata to track the list of records in each batch, and set a lifecycle policy to delete data succeeding 120 days.

explanation: DynamoDB is built for millions of small items with single-digit millisecond access, and its TTL feature deletes expired items automatically at no additional write cost, which exactly matches the 120-day retention requirement. Option A stores each tiny record as its own S3 object, which is expensive in PUT requests and gives poor retrieval latency. Option C requires managing a relational instance plus a custom deletion job that consumes capacity nightly. Option D reduces request cost through batching but sacrifices the low-latency access to individual records that the requirement demands.

question: A retail company is hosting an e-commerce website on AWS across multiple AWS Regions. The company wants to ensure the website remains operational at all times, especially for online purchases. The website stores data in an RDS MySQL instance. What solution will provide the highest availability for the database? (Note: the source book prints this as 'Choose two' but its answer key identifies a single correct option.)

options.text: Configure automated backups for Amazon RDS. In case of disruption, promote an automated backup to be a standalone DB instance and direct database traffic to it. Create a replacement read replica from the promoted DB instance.
Configure global tables and read replicas on Amazon RDS. Activate the cross-region scope. In case of disruption, use AWS Lambda to copy the read replicas to another region.
Set up global tables and automated backups on Amazon RDS. In case of disruption, use AWS Lambda to copy the read replicas to another region.

Set up read replicas for Amazon RDS. In case of disruption, promote a cross-Region read replica to a standalone DB instance. Direct database traffic to the promoted DB instance and create a new read replica based on it.

explanation: A cross-Region read replica stays continuously synchronised with the primary and can be promoted to a standalone writable instance in minutes, giving the lowest recovery time and recovery point objectives available for RDS MySQL across Regions. Option A restores from backup, which is far slower and loses data back to the last backup point. Options B and C both reference global tables, which is a DynamoDB feature and does not exist for RDS MySQL, so they are invalid on their face.

question: Example Corp. operates an on-premises data center connected to a VPC (VPC A) in its AWS account via an AWS Site-to-Site VPN. The on-premises network successfully accesses resources in VPC A. Subsequent to acquiring any company that has a separate VPC (VPC B) with no overlapping IP address ranges, Example Corp. established a VPC peering connection between VPC A and VPC B. What is the most efficient way for Example Corp. to enable its on-premises servers to access resources in VPC B?

options.text: Create a transit gateway. Attach the Site-to-Site VPN, VPC A, and VPC B to the transit gateway. Update the transit gateway route tables for all networks to add IP range routes for all other networks.

Create a transit gateway and a Site-to-Site VPN connection between the on-premises network and VPC B. Connect the VPN to the transit gateway. Add a route to direct traffic to the peered VPCs, and add an authorization rule to allow clients to access both VPCs A and B.
Update the route tables for the Site-to-Site VPN and both VPCs to include routes for all three networks. Configure BGP propagation for all three networks and wait for the propagation to complete.
Modify the Site-to-Site VPN's virtual private gateway to include both VPC A and VPC B. Split the two routers of the virtual private gateway between the two VPCs.

explanation: VPC peering is explicitly non-transitive: traffic arriving at VPC A over the VPN cannot traverse the peering connection into VPC B. Transit Gateway solves this by acting as a central router, with the VPN and both VPCs attached and route tables populated so on-premises traffic reaches either VPC. Option C fails because no amount of route table or BGP configuration can defeat the non-transitivity of peering. Option B adds a redundant second VPN and mixes in Client VPN authorisation rules that do not apply here. Option D is not possible, since a virtual private gateway attaches to exactly one VPC.

question: A company has migrated from an on-premises data center to AWS using a replatforming strategy. The application sends outbound email messages using a legacy Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) service that does not support TLS encryption. The company decides to replace this service with Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) and decommission the legacy SMTP server. The domain has been validated in SES, and limits have been lifted. How should the company modify the application to send email messages from Amazon SES?

options.text: Configure the application to connect to Amazon SES using TLS Wrapper. Create an IAM role with ses:SendEmail and ses:SendRawEmail permissions and attach it to an Amazon EC2 instance.
Configure the application to connect to Amazon SES using STARTTLS. Obtain Amazon SES SMTP credentials and use them to authenticate with Amazon SES.
Configure the application to use the SES API to send email messages. Create an IAM role with ses:SendEmail and ses:SendRawEmail permissions, and use the IAM role as a service role for Amazon SES.
Configure the application to use AWS SDKs to send email messages. Create an IAM user for Amazon SES, generate API access keys, and use these keys to authenticate with Amazon SES.

explanation: The requirement is to keep the application's SMTP integration while replacing the legacy server, so the minimal change is to point it at the SES SMTP interface using dedicated SES SMTP credentials, with STARTTLS upgrading the connection to TLS on the standard submission port. Option A uses TLS Wrapper, which is valid for SES but pairs it with an IAM role, which does not authenticate SMTP connections; SMTP requires SES SMTP credentials. Options C and D both switch the application to the SES API or SDK, a code change beyond what replatforming intends, and option C also misuses the concept of a service role.

question: A company has consolidated several AWS accounts into one organization using AWS Organizations. The finance team needs to generate a cost report that groups costs for all teams. The acquiring company wants a self-managed application to report costs. What solution will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an AWS Cost and Usage Report for the organization. Define tags and cost categories in the report. Create an Amazon Athena table based on the report and generate an Amazon QuickSight dataset for the finance team.
Create an AWS Cost and Usage Report for the organization. Define tags and cost categories in the report. Create a template in AWS Cost Explorer that the finance department will use to build reports.
Create an Amazon QuickSight dataset that receives spending information from the AWS Price List Query API and share the dataset with the finance team.
Use the AWS Price List Query API to collect account spending information. Create a template in AWS Cost Explorer for the finance team to build reports.

explanation: The AWS Cost and Usage Report is the authoritative, line-item source of organisation-wide spend, and defining tags and cost categories lets it be grouped by team. From there the finance team can either query the report through Athena and visualise it in QuickSight, or work from a Cost Explorer report template, both of which the answer key accepts. Options C and D fail because the AWS Price List Query API returns public service pricing, not actual account consumption, so it cannot report what the organisation has spent.

question: An organization operates an IoT platform hosted on AWS, where sensors from multiple locations transmit data to the company's Node.js API servers. These servers are deployed on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The incoming data is stored in an Amazon RDS MySQL database instance, which is configured with 4 TB of General Purpose SSD storage. Due to an increasing number of sensors, the API servers are overloaded, and RDS metrics show high write latency. Which steps will resolve the issues and allow future growth? (Choose two.)

options.text: Expand the MySQL General Purpose SSD storage to 6 TB to enhance the volume's IOPS performance.
Transition the database tier to Amazon Aurora and incorporate read replicas for better scalability and availability.
Utilize Amazon Kinesis Data Streams alongside AWS Lambda to manage the ingestion and processing of raw data.
Implement AWS X-Ray to diagnose application performance issues and scale up the number of API servers to handle the traffic load effectively.
Re-architect the database tier to use Amazon DynamoDB instead of RDS MySQL.

explanation: Two bottlenecks need addressing. Kinesis Data Streams with Lambda decouples sensor ingestion from the API tier, buffering bursts so the servers are no longer overwhelmed and scaling with sensor growth. Migrating to Aurora raises write throughput substantially over RDS MySQL on gp2 and adds read replicas for query offload and availability. Option A adds IOPS through capacity but only linearly and does not remove the architectural bottleneck. Option D diagnoses and scales the same overloaded design without decoupling ingestion. Option E is a wholesale rewrite of the data model, far more disruptive than the requirement calls for.

question: A company is building a serverless electronic document management system in the AWS region eu-central-1. The system uses Amazon CloudFront for content delivery, Amazon S3 for document storage, and Amazon API Gateway to call AWS Lambda functions. The Lambda functions interact with an Amazon Aurora Serverless database to store metadata. As the company expands outside Europe, the website needs to improve latency for users outside the region. Which of the following actions will meet the company's latency requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the S3 bucket and ensure the web application uses signed URLs for transfer acceleration.
Create an accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator and associate it with the CloudFront distribution.
Switch the API Gateway from regional endpoints to edge-optimized endpoints to reduce latency globally.
Deploy the system in multiple AWS regions, using global databases in Aurora Serverless to replicate data.
Introduce an Amazon RDS Proxy between the Lambda functions and the Aurora Serverless database to improve performance.

explanation: The book's answer key selects A and B. Transfer Acceleration improves document upload and download latency for users far from eu-central-1 by routing through the nearest edge location, and Global Accelerator provides anycast entry points onto the AWS backbone. Note that option C, switching API Gateway to edge-optimised endpoints, is the change most practitioners would make first for global API latency, and pairing Global Accelerator with CloudFront is not a standard pattern since CloudFront already terminates at edge locations, so this item is worth reviewing critically. Option D is a much larger multi-Region rebuild, and option E addresses connection pooling rather than geographic latency.

question: An adventure company allows users to upload photos and videos of their hiking and rafting activities through a mobile app. The media is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket in S3 Standard storage, and CloudFront serves the content. The company wants to optimize storage costs because most of the uploaded photos and videos are infrequently accessed after 30 days, but some are accessed frequently even later than that. What is the most cost-effective solution to meet this requirement while maintaining low latency?

options.text: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the S3 bucket to automatically move objects between frequent and infrequent access tiers based on usage.
Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition image and video objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive succeeding 30 days.
Replace S3 with Amazon EFS and mount it on Amazon EC2 instances for file system access.
Add a Cache-Control: max-age header to the S3 media files and set the cache duration to 30 days.

explanation: The access pattern is unpredictable at the object level: most media goes cold after 30 days but some stays hot. S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors each object individually and moves it between the frequent and infrequent access tiers automatically, with no retrieval fees and no latency penalty, which is exactly the case it was designed for. Option B sends everything to Deep Archive regardless of access, so the still-popular objects would incur multi-hour retrieval times. Option C replaces object storage with a far more expensive file system and adds EC2 instances. Option D tunes caching behaviour and does nothing to reduce storage cost.

question: A company has deployed cloud infrastructure in AWS and wants to define its infrastructure as code. The company plans to expand into multiple regions and accounts. What is the most effective solution to manage the infrastructure across regions and accounts?

options.text: Use AWS CloudFormation templates and IAM policies to control access across accounts, deploying templates in multiple regions.
Use AWS Organizations with AWS Control Tower to manage multi-account deployments and deploy CloudFormation templates from the management account.
Use AWS Organizations and AWS CloudFormation StackSets to deploy templates across accounts, ensuring necessary IAM permissions are in place.
Implement nested CloudFormation stacks and configure regions by modifying the nested stacks to deploy infrastructure.

explanation: CloudFormation StackSets is purpose-built to deploy a single template across many accounts and Regions from one operation, and its service-managed permissions model integrates directly with AWS Organizations so new accounts can be enrolled automatically. Option A requires deploying each stack manually per account and Region. Option B addresses landing zone governance and account provisioning but is not itself the multi-account deployment mechanism for application infrastructure. Option D uses nested stacks, which modularise a single stack within one account and Region and do nothing for cross-account distribution.

question: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances that needs access to an Amazon Aurora DB cluster. The EC2 instances are part of one security group, and the DB cluster uses a different security group. The company needs to ensure that only the application can access the DB cluster while adhering to least privilege access. Which of the following actions will achieve this while maintaining security? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add an inbound rule to the EC2 instances' security group, specifying the DB cluster's security group as the source over the default Aurora port.
Configure an outbound rule in the EC2 instances' security group to allow traffic directed to the database cluster's security group on the default Aurora port.
Add an inbound rule to the DB cluster's security group, specifying the EC2 instances' security group as the source over the default Aurora port.
Define an outbound rule in the database cluster's security group to allow traffic directed to the EC2 instances' security group on the default Aurora port.
Establish an outbound rule in the database cluster's security group to allow traffic directed to the EC2 instances' security group on ephemeral ports.

explanation: The book's answer key selects A and C. Option C is the essential control: the database security group must permit inbound traffic on port 3306 with the EC2 security group referenced as the source, which is the least-privilege way to scope access to exactly the application instances. Note that security groups are stateful, so response traffic is automatically allowed and no outbound rule is required, which correctly eliminates options B, D and E. Option A as printed grants inbound access on the EC2 side from the database, which is not what the traffic flow requires, so this item is worth reviewing critically; the more defensible pairing would be C plus an outbound rule on the EC2 security group.

question: A video processing company wants to build a machine learning model using 600 TB of compressed data stored in on-premises network-attached storage. The company lacks the compute resources on-premises to process the data and wants to use AWS for machine learning experiments. The company needs to transfer the data to AWS within three weeks, with encryption in transit. Which solution will meet the data transfer requirements most cost-effectively?

options.text: Order several AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices. Configure the devices with a destination S3 bucket, transfer the data to the devices, and then ship the devices to AWS.
Set up a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect link to the nearest AWS Region and transfer the data over a VPN connection to Amazon S3.
Set up a VPN connection between the on-premises storage and AWS and transfer the data via the VPN connection.
Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway on-premises. Configure it to transfer the data to Amazon S3.

explanation: At 600 TB, physical transfer wins on both time and cost. Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices hold roughly 80 TB usable each, encrypt data at rest and in transit with AES-256, and several run in parallel comfortably inside three weeks. Option B is doubtful on timeline because provisioning a new Direct Connect circuit typically takes weeks before any data moves, and the data transfer charges are substantial. Option C over a VPN would take months at typical internet bandwidth and would saturate the company's link. Option D still moves all 600 TB over the existing internet connection, with the same bandwidth constraint.

question: A company allows employees to work remotely through a VPN and needs access to internal applications hosted in VPCs across multiple AWS accounts. Currently, applications are accessible from an on-premises office via an AWS Site-to-Site VPN. VPCs in the main account are peered with others. The company wants a scalable and cost-effective AWS Client VPN solution. What is the best solution to meet these requirements?

options.text: Set up a Client VPN endpoint in each AWS account and configure routing to internal applications.
Deploy a Client VPN endpoint in the primary AWS account and configure routing to internal applications in peered VPCs.
Deploy a Client VPN endpoint in the main AWS account, connect to a transit gateway, and configure routing to internal applications across accounts.
Use a Client VPN endpoint in the main AWS account and establish connectivity to the existing Site-to-Site VPN for internal application access.

explanation: A single Client VPN endpoint associated with a Transit Gateway attachment reaches every attached VPC across all accounts through the transit gateway's route tables, which is both scalable and the cheapest option since Client VPN is billed per endpoint association and per connection hour. Option B fails on the non-transitivity of VPC peering: the Client VPN endpoint cannot route through a peered VPC to reach another. Option A multiplies endpoint costs and administrative burden by the number of accounts. Option D misapplies the Site-to-Site VPN, which connects the office network rather than remote individual clients.

question: An enterprise using AWS Organizations wants developers to access third-party software from AWS Marketplace, restricted to an approved list via Private Marketplace. The procurement team, with a specific IAM role, will manage this. Administration of Private Marketplace must be denied for all other users and roles. How should the architecture be designed to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create the procurement-manager role in all accounts and attach AWSPrivateMarketplaceAdminFullAccess. Deny other administrative permissions with an SCP at the organizational root.

Set up the procurement-manager role in shared service accounts only, granting AWSPrivateMarketplaceAdminFullAccess. Add an SCP to deny all other Private Marketplace admin permissions and role creation.
Deploy procurement-manager role in all accounts with PowerUserAccess and deny AWSPrivateMarketplaceAdminFullAccess for all other IAM users via inline policies.
Assign procurement-manager role with AdministratorAccess in all accounts. Use permissions boundaries to limit admin actions related to Private Marketplace.

explanation: Confining the procurement-manager role to shared service accounts limits the blast radius, while an SCP that denies Private Marketplace administration for every other principal, and denies creation of roles that could circumvent it, enforces the restriction organisation-wide regardless of local account permissions. Option A creates the privileged role in every account, widening exposure unnecessarily. Option C relies on inline policies attached account by account, which is unenforceable at scale and easily bypassed. Option D grants AdministratorAccess, a gross violation of least privilege, and permissions boundaries constrain identities rather than preventing other principals from acting.

question: A company is migrating its on-premises order-processing system to AWS with minimal application changes. It includes a web front end on VMs, RabbitMQ for messaging, and Kubernetes for backend processing. Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Create an EC2 Auto Scaling group for the web front end using an AMI and Application Load Balancer. Replace RabbitMQ with Amazon MQ, and run the backend on Amazon EKS.
Replace the web front end with an API Gateway and use custom Lambda runtimes. Replace RabbitMQ with Amazon MQ, and host the backend on Amazon EKS.
Deploy the web front end on an EC2 Auto Scaling group using an AMI. Replace RabbitMQ with Amazon MQ. Host the backend on a custom Kubernetes setup on EC2 instances.
Use an EC2 Auto Scaling group for the web front end. Replace RabbitMQ with Amazon SQS and run the backend on Amazon EKS.

explanation: Each component maps to its closest managed equivalent, which is what minimal application change plus least operational overhead requires. The VM-based web tier lifts to EC2 behind an ALB, Amazon MQ runs RabbitMQ as a managed broker so messaging code is unchanged, and EKS provides managed Kubernetes for the existing backend workloads. Option B rewrites the front end for Lambda, a significant application change. Option C keeps a self-managed Kubernetes cluster, retaining the operational burden EKS removes. Option D swaps RabbitMQ for SQS, which uses a different protocol and API and would force application changes.

question: A company plans to migrate its .NET-based three-tier application with a MySQL database to AWS to handle 200,000 daily users. The architecture must be scalable and highly available. What steps should be taken for this migration?

options.text: Deploy the application with AWS Elastic Beanstalk, an EC2 Auto Scaling group in multiple AZs, and an RDS MySQL Multi-AZ instance. Use a Network Load Balancer and Route 53 for traffic management.
Use CloudFormation to launch an Application Load Balancer (ALB) with an EC2 Auto Scaling group across three AZs. Deploy a Multi-AZ Aurora MySQL cluster with Route 53 for DNS.
Use Elastic Beanstalk to span the application across two Regions with an ALB in each. Deploy a Multi-AZ Aurora MySQL cluster with a cross-region replica. Use Route 53 for traffic distribution.
Use CloudFormation to deploy an ALB with an ECS cluster of Spot instances and an RDS MySQL instance. Manage DNS with Route 53.

explanation: The book's answer key selects A: Elastic Beanstalk has first-class .NET on Windows support and handles provisioning, deployment and health monitoring, an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones provides scalability, and RDS MySQL Multi-AZ delivers database high availability with automatic failover. Note that an Application Load Balancer would normally be preferred over a Network Load Balancer for a web application tier, so that detail is worth scrutinising. Option C spans two Regions, which exceeds the stated requirement and adds substantial cost. Option D relies on Spot instances for a production user-facing tier and a single-AZ RDS instance, failing the high-availability requirement.

question: A company plans to refactor its EC2-based web application into microservices using containers. The application exists in production and testing environments, with known load patterns. Operational complexity should be minimized. What is the most cost-effective serverless architecture for this refactor?

options.text: Convert the application into Lambda functions with concurrency limits and integrate with API Gateway for separate production and testing environments.
Use Elastic Container Service (ECS) with Fargate, deploying production and testing tasks from ECR. Route traffic with two Application Load Balancers.
Deploy Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) with Fargate for production and testing environments, and route traffic using two Application Load Balancers.
Host the containers on Elastic Beanstalk with separate environments for production and testing. Use two Application Load Balancers for routing.

explanation: ECS with Fargate runs containers without any server or cluster management and is the lowest-complexity serverless container platform on AWS, with images pulled from ECR and separate ALBs isolating production from testing. Option A abandons the containerisation goal entirely and forces a rewrite into functions. Option C also uses Fargate but adds the Kubernetes control plane, which carries an hourly charge and considerable operational complexity that the requirement asks to avoid. Option D keeps Elastic Beanstalk's managed EC2 instances underneath, so it is not serverless and costs more for known steady load patterns.
